summary: Specifies how point-to-multipoint BFD is supported in TRILL (Transparent Interconnection of Lots of Links). As with TRILL point-to-point BFD, control packets are carried using RBridge Channel messages. It updates RFC 7175 and RFC 7177 and is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: TRILL is a way of linking bridges together. This document lets one bridge quickly check the health of the paths to many other bridges at once.

questions: how does bfd work in trill
subtitle: How a TRILL bridge can check, with one multicast probe stream, that its multicast paths to many other bridges still work.

tldr.problem: Applications that rely on TRILL multicast need to notice quickly when multicast delivery fails. Existing TRILL BFD only covered point-to-point sessions, and its packets are dropped if the multicast M bit is set.
tldr.mechanism: A new RBridge Channel message, P2MP BFD Control (protocol code point 0x007), carries multipoint BFD Control packets over TRILL multicast. Tails demultiplex on source address, My Discriminator and Data Label, and report lost connectivity to the head with unicast BFD.
tldr.outcome: TRILL gains support for P2MP BFD as defined in RFC 8562. The document is on the standards track and updates RFC 7175 and RFC 7177.

today: RFC 8564 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted or updated. It updates RFC 7175 and RFC 7177.

sections.title: Why TRILL Needs P2MP BFD
sections.content:
TRILL supports multicast forwarding. Applications built on TRILL multicast may need to detect multicast failures quickly, and the tool for that is point-to-multipoint (P2MP) BFD from RFC 8562. This RFC specifies how TRILL supports it.

The head end periodically sends BFD Control packets to all tails using TRILL multicast. A new RBridge Channel message is allocated for this purpose. To run the global protection of distribution used for multicast forwarding, the head also needs to track the active status of tails, as described in RFC 8563.

If a tail stops receiving the new message from the head, it should tell the head about the lack of multipoint connectivity. It does so with unicast BFD Control packets, sent using the existing RBridge Channel message for BFD Control from RFC 7175.
sections.plainLanguage: One bridge keeps shouting 'I am still here' to many others. Anyone who stops hearing it quietly tells the shouter.

sections.title: Bootstrapping Sessions
sections.content:
The TRILL adjacency mechanism bootstraps one-hop TRILL BFD sessions, as described in RFC 7177. Multi-hop sessions are expected to be configured by the network manager.

One small wording change to RFC 7177 is needed. The second sentence of its Section 6 used to say that an RBridge supporting BFD learns whether a neighbor has BFD enabled from the BFD-Enabled TLV in its Hellos. It now says that an RBridge supporting BFD (see RFC 7175 and RFC 8564) learns this in the same way. A normative reference to this document is added to RFC 7177 as a result.
sections.plainLanguage: Neighbors who are next door find each other automatically. Farther-away partners have to be set up by hand by the person running the network.

sections.title: The New RBridge Channel Message
sections.content:
RFC 7175 defines RBridge Channel protocol number 0x002 for point-to-point BFD Control packets. It says such a packet is generally dropped if the M bit in the TRILL Header is nonzero. A P2MP head probes tails by multicast, so the M bit will be 1.

For that reason this document defines a new RBridge Channel message, P2MP BFD Control, with protocol code point 0x007. An RBridge that supports P2MP BFD MUST support this message. The capability is announced in the RBridge Channel Protocols sub-TLV in Link State PDUs (LSPs), per RFC 7176.

As specified in RFC 7178, a tail that receives these TRILL Data packets absorbs them itself rather than delivering them to attached end stations.
sections.plainLanguage: The old message was for talking to one friend and was thrown away if sent to a crowd. So a new kind of message was made just for talking to a crowd.

sections.title: Discriminators and Demultiplexing
sections.content:
Processing follows Section 3.2 of RFC 7175, except that the M bit test is reversed. If the M bit is zero, the packet MUST be discarded. If it is one, the packet is processed.

The tail then demultiplexes incoming BFD packets using the source address and My Discriminator, as in RFC 8562. TRILL adds a requirement: the tail must also use the Data Label (the inner VLAN or the Fine-Grained Label from RFC 7172).

If the tail has to tell the head that a multipath has failed, it MUST send unicast BFD Control packets using the same Data Label the head used.
sections.plainLanguage: A tail sorts incoming messages by who sent them, which number they carry and which group they belong to. It answers using the same group name it heard.

sections.title: Tracking Active Tails
sections.content:
Under RFC 8562, the head has a session of type MultipointHead bound to a multipoint path. It sends multipoint BFD Control packets over that path and receives none. Each tail dynamically creates a MultipointTail session for each multipoint path, and these sessions receive the head's packets.

A multicast tree root that needs to keep track of all receivers can maintain a MultipointClient session per receiver of interest, as described in RFC 8563. This RFC leaves the detailed operation of tracking active tails to that document.
sections.plainLanguage: The head keeps a roll call of the listeners it cares about, and each listener keeps a note of which shouting head it is hearing.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Multipoint BFD has its own authentication but no encryption. Here, the P2MP BFD payloads travel in RBridge Channel messages that RFC 7978 extended to provide security. RFC 7978 gives encryption only for point-to-point extended messages, so its encryption does not apply here. Its authentication is stronger than what BFD offers, so there is little reason to use BFD's own mechanisms when RFC 7978 authentication is in use.

The RFC expects a future TRILL document to provide group keying. At that point RBridge Channel security would offer both encryption and authentication.
sections.plainLanguage: The messages can be signed so that nobody can fake them, but for now they cannot be locked in a box when sent to a whole crowd.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: IANA allocated one value from the Standards Action range of the 'RBridge Channel Protocols' registry, part of the TRILL Parameters registry: P2MP BFD Control, number 0x007.
sections.plainLanguage: The official list of message types got one new entry, number 7, for the crowd-talking message.
